Representative mammalian species include the white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus), black bear (Euarctos americanus), bobcat (Lynx rufus), grey fox (Urocyon cinereoargenteus), raccoon (Procyon lotor), opossum (Didelphis virginiana), striped skunk (Mephitis mephitis), cotton rat (Sigmodon hispidus), and eastern grey squirrel (Sciurus carolinensis). Typical birds include the wild turkey (Meleagris gallopavo), ruffed grouse (Bonasa umbellus), blue jay (Cyanocitta cristata), brown creeper (Certhia familiaris), Carolina wren (Thryothorus ludovicianus), catbird (Dumetella carolinensis), wood thrush, (Hylocichla mustelina), veery (Hylocichla fuscescens), Kentucky warbler (Oporornis formosus), common grackle (Quiscalus quiscula), scarlet tanager (Prianaza olivacea), and slatecolored junco (Junco hyemalis).
The activities of man have greatly influenced the present composition of the forest through repeated timber harvest programs and associated logging and access road construction. The Applicant reports that the last major logging activity took place during late 1966 through early 1968 when 12 inch DBH (diameter breast height) trees having 16 feet of clear log were harvested.
Second growth vegetation predominates throughout the area. The effect upon the forest community has been to favor faunal species benefiting from early seral stages and the corresponding depression of wildlife populations adapted to climax forest conditions. As a consequence of past land use practices, the reestablished white-tailed deer have been favored as have ruffed grouse; whereas turkey, squirrel, and the pileated woodpecker (Dryocopus pileatus) have been subjected to less favorable environments.
Rough topography typified by upland slopes, ridges, moist coves, and intervening stream drainages provides a complex of macro- and micro-environments offering a desirable mix of food, water, and escape cover favorable to the perpetuation of a wild land fauna rich in its species diversity. Some of the cold-blooded vertebrates, particularly the amphibians, may be restricted to quite local habitats in moist coves, forested ravines, or rock outcropping. This is particularly true of the Jordan's salamander (Plethodon jordani), which favors moist areas on north facing slopes, and other amphibian species described in Subsection 2.2.3. In contrast, bear, feral pig (Sus scrofa), and other wildlife may range widely over remote areas significantly larger than the proposed project boundary.
